claim: SAI afferents encode shape and texture.
source: These vertebrate touch receptors, which innervate Merkel cells, encode shape and texture.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SAI afferents in the abstract.

claim: SAI afferents displayed a high degree of variability in touch-evoked firing and peripheral anatomy.
source: SAI afferents displayed a high degree of variability in touch-evoked firing and peripheral anatomy.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental observations.

claim: The arrangement of mechanotransduction sites at heminodes is a key structural feature that accounts in part for an afferent's firing properties.
source: A systematic survey of arbor configurations predicted that the arrangement of mechanotransduction sites at heminodes is a key structural feature that accounts in part for an afferent's firing properties.
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling experiments.

claim: Mammalian mechanosensory afferents are tuned to extract specific features of a tactile stimulus and encode them as trains of action potentials with unique firing properties.
source: In mammals, distinct classes of mechanosensory afferents are tuned to extract specific features of a tactile stimulus and then to encode them as trains of action potentials, or spikes, with unique firing properties (Johnson, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Johnson, 2001.

claim: Mouse hair follicles are innervated by at least three molecularly distinct types of cutaneous afferents.
source: For example, recent studies show that mouse hair follicles are innervated by at least three molecularly (Li et al., 2011) and 10 anatomically (Wu et al., 2012) distinct types of cutaneous afferents.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Mouse hair follicles are innervated by 10 anatomically distinct types of cutaneous afferents.
source: For example, recent studies show that mouse hair follicles are innervated by at least three molecularly (Li et al., 2011) and 10 anatomically (Wu et al., 2012) distinct types of cutaneous afferents.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2012.

claim: Somatosensory neurons do not initiate action potentials at axon initial segments.
source: Due to their unusual architecture, somatosensory neurons do not initiate action potentials at axon initial segments, as do neurons of the central nervous system.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about somatosensory neurons.

claim: Spikes initiate at the heminode in Pacinian corpuscles.
source: For myelinated tactile afferents, a landmark study of Pacinian corpuscles established that spikes initiate at the heminode, the most distal node of Ranvier (Loewenstein and Rathkamp, 1958).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Loewenstein and Rathkamp, 1958.

claim: A Pacinian corpuscle is innervated by an un-branched afferent.
source: A Pacinian corpuscle is innervated by an un-branched afferent; however, most tactile end organs comprise branching afferents with multiple sites of sensory transduction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Pacinian corpuscles.

claim: Most tactile end organs comprise branching afferents with multiple sites of sensory transduction.
source: A Pacinian corpuscle is innervated by an un-branched afferent; however, most tactile end organs comprise branching afferents with multiple sites of sensory transduction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about tactile end organs.

claim: Merkel cell-neurite complexes are required to produce canonical SAI firing patterns in mouse touch-dome afferents.
source: The SAI afferent's end organ is a cluster of Merkel cell-neurite complexes, which are required to produce canonical SAI firing patterns in mouse touch-dome afferents (Maricich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maricich et al., 2009.

claim: SAI afferents are myelinated Aβ afferents that innervate Merkel cells located in the epidermis.
source: SAI afferents are myelinated Aβ afferents that innervate Merkel cells located in the epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SAI afferents.

claim: SAI afferents lose their myelin sheaths just below the dermal–epidermal junction.
source: Although dermal segments are thickly myelinated, SAI afferents lose their myelin sheaths just below the dermal–epidermal junction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citation to Iggo and Muir, 1969.

claim: NaV1.6 localized to 93% of observed myelin end points in SAI afferents.
source: In SAI afferents, NaV1.6 puncta localized to 93% of observed myelin end points (N = 28/30, Figure 1B) and 100% of myelin gaps (N = 9/9, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from immunostaining and quantification, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: NaV1.6 localized to 100% of myelin gaps in SAI afferents.
source: In SAI afferents, NaV1.6 puncta localized to 93% of observed myelin end points (N = 28/30, Figure 1B) and 100% of myelin gaps (N = 9/9, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from immunostaining and quantification, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: NaV1.6 is a principal node component in SAI afferents.
source: These data demonstrate that nodes and heminodes in SAI afferents can be reliably identified by visualizing either MBP or NaV1.6. Moreover, they identify NaV1.6 as a principal node component in these cutaneous afferents.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunostaining data showing NaV1.6 localization.

claim: Voltage-activated sodium or potassium channels were not observed in unmyelinated neurites juxtaposed to Merkel cells.
source: We did not observe immunoreactivity against voltage-activated sodium or potassium channels in unmyelinated neurites juxtaposed to Merkel cells (N = 201 Merkel cell-neurite complexes), although it is possible that these channels are present at levels below detection threshold.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from immunostaining.

claim: Spikes likely initiate at heminodes in SAI afferents.
source: Based on the strong enrichment of NaV1.6 at heminodes, we infer that spikes likely initiate at these sites, as they do in Pacinian corpuscles (Loewenstein and Rathkamp, 1958), rather than initiating in SAI-afferent terminals.
evidence: This is inferred from the NaV1.6 localization data and comparison to Pacinian corpuscles.

claim: In 83% of touch domes surveyed, Merkel cells were innervated by branches of a single SAI afferent.
source: In 83% of touch domes surveyed, Merkel cells were innervated by branches of a single SAI afferent (N = 18, Figure 1D–D',F–F'; Video 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from 3D reconstructions.

claim: In three reconstructions, two afferents projecting from different nerve trunks contacted Merkel cells within a single touch dome.
source: In three reconstructions, two afferents projecting from different nerve trunks contacted Merkel cells within a single touch dome (Figure 1E–E'; Video 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from 3D reconstructions.

claim: SAI afferents displayed five to seven nested orders of branches.
source: Afferents displayed five to seven nested orders of branches.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of reconstructed touch domes.

claim: Arbor complexity did not correlate with Merkel-cell number.
source: Arbor complexity, as represented by the highest branching order, did not correlate with Merkel-cell number (Figure 1G), which ranged almost fivefold (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Most Merkel cells (>85%) were directly contacted by neurites.
source: Most Merkel cells (>85%) were directly contacted by neurites, suggesting that they were incorporated into afferent arbors (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ≥80% of terminal neurites were occupied by Merkel cells in most touch domes.
source: Similarly, ≥80% of terminal neurites were occupied by Merkel cells in most touch domes (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Individual heminodes receive inputs from multiple Merkel cell–neurite complexes.
source: Given that the number of complexes exceeded heminodes within each arbor, we reasoned that individual heminodes must receive inputs from multiple Merkel cell–neurite complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative data showing more complexes than heminodes.

claim: Most Merkel cells were arranged individually on terminal neurites (70%).
source: Most Merkel cells were arranged individually on terminal neurites (70%, N = 165, Figure 2B,C), although chains of three or more Merkel cells along individual neurites were occasionally observed (Figure 2B,D; Ebara et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: During sustained touch, SAI afferents produce a biphasic spike train characterized by high-frequency firing during stimulus onset and low-frequency firing with a highly variable interspike interval during sustained displacement.
source: During sustained touch, SAI afferents produce a biphasic spike train characterized by high-frequency firing during stimulus onset (ramp phase) and low-frequency firing with a highly variable interspike interval (ISI) during sustained displacement (static phase).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SAI afferent responses.

claim: Touch-evoked firing rates and mechanical sensitivity vary considerably between individual SAI afferents.
source: Touch-evoked firing rates and mechanical sensitivity vary considerably between individual SAI afferents (Mountcastle et al., 1966; Goodwin et al., 1995; Wellnitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mountcastle et al., 1966; Goodwin et al., 1995; Wellnitz et al., 2010.

claim: First spike latencies were significantly shorter in large touch domes compared with small touch domes for suprathreshold stimuli.
source: As predicted, first spike latencies were significantly shorter in large touch domes (mean ± SEM, 10.9 ± 1.6 ms, N = 57) compared with small touch domes (40.0 ± 14.5 ms, N = 60; p = 0.027; Student's t test, one-tailed) for suprathreshold stimuli.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Having more Merkel cell–neurite complexes in a touch dome results in a faster response during dynamic indentation.
source: These data suggest that having more Merkel cell–neurite complexes in a touch dome results in a faster response during dynamic indentation.
evidence: This is inferred from the first spike latency data.

claim: The variance of first spike latencies was significantly higher in small touch domes.
source: We also noted that the variance of first spike latencies was significantly higher in small touch domes (p<0.0001; two-sample F test, two-tailed), which suggests that SAI afferents with fewer transduction units display less reliable spike timing during dynamic stimulation.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: SAI afferents with fewer transduction units display less reliable spike timing during dynamic stimulation.
source: We also noted that the variance of first spike latencies was significantly higher in small touch domes (p<0.0001; two-sample F test, two-tailed), which suggests that SAI afferents with fewer transduction units display less reliable spike timing during dynamic stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the variance data.

claim: Mechanical sensitivity differed significantly between SAI afferents innervating mouse touch domes.
source: This analysis confirmed that mechanical sensitivity differed significantly between SAI afferents innervating mouse touch domes (κ = 2.1–14.2 mm−1; p < 0.0001, Extra sum-of-squares F test); however, this measure did not scale with total Merkel-cell number.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of displacement-response relations.

claim: Mechanical sensitivity did not scale with total Merkel-cell number.
source: This analysis confirmed that mechanical sensitivity differed significantly between SAI afferents innervating mouse touch domes (κ = 2.1–14.2 mm−1; p < 0.0001, Extra sum-of-squares F test); however, this measure did not scale with total Merkel-cell number.
evidence: This is based on analysis of displacement-response relations.

claim: 19 SAI afferents innervated individual touch domes in adult mouse hindlimb.
source: We found that 19 SAI afferents innervated individual touch domes, six innervated two touch domes each and two afferents innervated three touch domes each.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Six SAI afferents innervated two touch domes each in adult mouse hindlimb.
source: We found that 19 SAI afferents innervated individual touch domes, six innervated two touch domes each and two afferents innervated three touch domes each.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Two SAI afferents innervated three touch domes each in adult mouse hindlimb.
source: We found that 19 SAI afferents innervated individual touch domes, six innervated two touch domes each and two afferents innervated three touch domes each.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The percentage of SAI afferents that innervate multiple touch domes in the hindlimb of adult mice (30%) is much lower than that reported in cats (>60%).
source: Thus, the percentage of SAI afferents that innervate multiple touch domes in the hindlimb of adult mice (30%) is much lower than that reported in cats (>60%; Tapper, 1965; Iggo and Muir, 1969) or mouse neonatal back skin (3/4 SAI afferents; Woodbury and Koerber, 2007).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data with cited literature.

claim: Skin mechanics did not account for differences in SAI-afferent sensitivity.
source: First, skin mechanics did not account for these differences because displacement–force relations were indistinguishable between these recordings (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of force-displacement data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The model's predicted spike-timing variability corresponded to the skewed Gaussian distribution previously reported for mouse SAI afferents.
source: The model's predicted spike-timing variability, assessed by the distribution of normalized ISIs during static-phase responses (black bars: N = 1,591 intervals), corresponded to the skewed Gaussian distribution previously reported for mouse SAI afferents (orange bars: N = 3,348 intervals from 11 afferents; Wellnitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison of model predictions with experimental data, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The model produced spike times that reproduced the dynamics of SAI responses over a range of stimulus conditions.
source: The model produced spike times that reproduced the dynamics of SAI responses over a range of stimulus conditions, including different displacement magnitudes and ramp accelerations.
evidence: This is based on model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Moving two transduction units to yield groupings of {10, 5, 1, 1} or {6, 5, 3, 3} were sufficient to significantly alter the shape of simulated displacement–response relations.
source: From the initial configuration of {8, 5, 3, 1}, we found that moving only two transduction units, to yield groupings of {10, 5, 1, 1} or {6, 5, 3, 3}, were sufficient to significantly alter the shape of simulated displacement–response relations.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling experiments.

claim: Increasing the primary cluster to 10 units increased firing rates for suprathreshold stimuli by 20%.
source: Increasing the primary cluster to 10 units increased firing rates for suprathreshold stimuli by 20%.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling experiments.

claim: Moving two transduction units from the largest group to the smallest decreased predicted firing rates for supra-threshold displacements by 25%.
source: Conversely, moving two transduction units from the largest group to the smallest decreased predicted firing rates for supra-threshold displacements by 25%.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling experiments.

claim: Firing rates increased 7.2% per transduction unit added to a primary cluster on average.
source: On average, firing rates increased 7.2% per transduction unit added to a primary cluster and 2.8% per transduction unit added to a secondary cluster.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling experiments across multiple arbor configurations.

claim: Firing rates increased 2.8% per transduction unit added to a secondary cluster on average.
source: On average, firing rates increased 7.2% per transduction unit added to a primary cluster and 2.8% per transduction unit added to a secondary cluster.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling experiments across multiple arbor configurations.

claim: Touch-evoked firing is increased when Merkel cell–neurite complexes are arranged in a skewed distribution among heminodes.
source: Collectively, these models predict that touch-evoked firing is increased when Merkel cell–neurite complexes are arranged in a skewed distribution among heminodes.
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling experiments.

claim: A tactile afferent with few transduction units can achieve high touch sensitivity by unevenly grouping transduction units to action potential initiation sites.
source: Thus, these simulations demonstrate that a tactile afferent with few transduction units can achieve high touch sensitivity by unevenly grouping transduction units to action potential initiation sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from computational modeling experiments comparing different arbor configurations.

claim: The skewed grouping strategy produced a significantly higher mechanical sensitivity than the evenly distributed end organ.
source: Despite having 40% fewer transduction units, the skewed grouping strategy produced a significantly higher mechanical sensitivity than the evenly distributed end organ (κ = 7.7 and 5.0, respectively, p = 0.005; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: This study is the first to construct computational models of mammalian tactile afferents that are constrained with structural parameters quantified from intact tactile end organs.
source: To our knowledge, this study is the first to construct computational models of mammalian tactile afferents that are constrained with structural parameters quantified from intact tactile end organs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's approach.

claim: Asymmetric clustering of transduction sites at spike initiation zones regulates mechanosensory coding in a branched tactile afferent.
source: Computational results predict that asymmetric clustering of transduction sites at spike initiation zones regulates mechanosensory coding in a branched tactile afferent.
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling experiments.

claim: NaV1.6 is the first sodium channel isoform localized in tactile end organs.
source: Our results are the first to localize NaV1.6 in tactile end organs, which extends previous reports that identified this isoform in unmyelinated nociceptors and as the principal sodium channel at central and peripheral nodes (Caldwell et al., 2000; Black et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study, supported by citations to previous work on NaV1.6 in other contexts.

claim: NaV1.6 confers rapid sodium channel kinetics and mediates resurgent currents in DRG neurons.
source: Thus, it is notable that NaV1.6 confers rapid sodium channel kinetics and mediates resurgent currents, which facilitate high-frequency firing, in DRG neurons (Herzog et al., 2003; Cummins et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herzog et al., 2003; Cummins et al., 2005.

claim: SAI afferents display unusually high instantaneous firing frequencies exceeding 1000 Hz.
source: SAI afferents display unusually high instantaneous firing frequencies exceeding 1000 Hz (Iggo and Muir, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iggo and Muir, 1969.

claim: The Gaussian distribution of Merkel cell connections to terminal neurites suggests that they are formed through probabilistic rather than deterministic mechanisms.
source: Although most terminal neurites innervate single Merkel cells, the Gaussian distribution of these connections suggests that they are formed through probabilistic rather than deterministic mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution analysis of Merkel cell connections.

claim: Touch-dome afferents display exuberant terminal branching in Atoh1 knockout mice, which lack Merkel cells.
source: Interestingly, touch-dome afferents display exuberant terminal branching in Atoh1 knockout mice, which lack Merkel cells (Maricich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maricich et al., 2009.

claim: Targeting and maintenance of touch-dome innervation is independent of Merkel cell-derived signals.
source: These findings suggest that targeting and maintenance of touch-dome innervation is independent of Merkel cell-derived signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of exuberant branching in Merkel cell knockout mice.

claim: Merkel-cell contacts are required for appropriate sprouting and/or pruning of touch-dome arbors.
source: Instead, we propose that Merkel-cell contacts are required for appropriate sprouting and/or pruning of touch-dome arbors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the data from Merkel cell knockout mice.

claim: The models presented here are the first to computationally represent the sequence of key events in tactile encoding: the conversion of touch at the skin's surface to mechanical distortion at tactile receptors, mechanoelectrical transduction and spike initiation at heminodes.
source: Thus, the models presented here are the first to computationally represent the sequence of key events in tactile encoding: the conversion of touch at the skin's surface to mechanical distortion at tactile receptors, mechanoelectrical transduction and spike initiation at heminodes.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the computational modeling approach.

claim: Viscoelastic skin relaxation occurs during sustained touch stimuli.
source: By contrast, viscoelastic skin relaxation occurs during sustained touch stimuli, such as those encoded by SAI afferents (Cohen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cohen et al., 1999.

claim: Primary clusters of Merkel cell–neurite complexes sometimes contained ≥50% of Merkel cells in the entire arbor.
source: Primary clusters of Merkel cell–neurite complexes, converging on a single heminode, sometimes contained ≥50% of Merkel cells in the entire arbor.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of reconstructed arbors.

claim: Changing the primary cluster size by as few as two Merkel cell–neurite complexes significantly altered afferent firing in computational simulations.
source: In computational simulations, changing the primary cluster size by as few as two Merkel cell–neurite complexes significantly altered afferent firing.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling experiments.

claim: The findings provide an anatomical correlate and a plausible biological mechanism to explain the driver effect observed in branched sensory afferents.
source: Nonetheless, our findings provide an anatomical correlate and a plausible biological mechanism to explain the driver effect observed in branched sensory afferents (Lindblom and Tapper, 1966; Horch et al., 1974; Fukami, 1980).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, supported by citations to previous work on the driver effect.

claim: The most sensitive receptor configuration consists of a single cluster of transduction sites connected to a single heminode.
source: Theoretically, the most sensitive receptor configuration consists of a single cluster of transduction sites connected to a single heminode, as found in invertebrate stretch receptors (Edwards and Ottoson, 1958).
evidence: This is stated as theoretical knowledge, supported by citation to Edwards and Ottoson, 1958.

claim: Distributing transduction complexes among multiple heminodes could serve as a safety feature by increasing robustness to injury.
source: First, given that the skin is our body's protective covering, this arrangement could serve as a safety feature by increasing robustness to injury.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed anatomical arrangement.

claim: Multiple spike initiation zones ensure high-fidelity signal propagation from branches located millimeters apart in cutaneous afferents with large receptive fields.
source: Second, for cutaneous afferents with large receptive fields, multiple spike initiation zones ensure high-fidelity signal propagation from branches located millimeters apart (Li et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to Li et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2012.

claim: An SAI afferent can innervate 2–5 touch domes, each spaced ∼0.7 mm apart.
source: For example, an SAI afferent can innervate 2–5 touch domes, each spaced ∼0.7 mm apart (Tapper, 1965; Iggo and Muir, 1969; Woodbury and Koerber, 2007; Wellnitz et al., 2010; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Heminodes were located within 19–41 µm of lanceolate endings innervating hair follicles.
source: We also noted that heminodes were located within 19–41 µm of lanceolate endings innervating hair follicles (N = 7 end organs).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Spike initiation zones in close proximity to end organs is a general feature of myelinated tactile afferents.
source: As individual rapidly adapting afferents can innervate tens to hundreds of hair follicles (Li et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2012), this observation suggests that spike initiation zones in close proximity to end organs is a general feature of myelinated tactile afferents.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of heminode locations, supported by citations.

claim: Distinct clusters might extend the receptor's range of sensory coding.
source: Third, distinct clusters might extend the receptor's range of sensory coding (Eagles and Purple, 1974).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Eagles and Purple, 1974.

claim: Individual muscle-spindle afferents are proposed to encode both dynamic and static stimuli by innervating distinct structures called bag and chain fibers.
source: For example, individual muscle-spindle afferents are proposed to encode both dynamic and static stimuli by innervating distinct structures called bag and chain fibers (Quick et al., 1980; Banks et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Quick et al., 1980; Banks et al., 1997.

claim: Some touch domes might be innervated by multiple sensory afferents.
source: Our reconstructions suggest that some touch domes might be innervated by multiple sensory afferents, and this likely contributes to the wide range of firing properties observed for SAI afferents.
evidence: This is inferred from the reconstruction data.

claim: SAI afferents with overlapping receptive fields have been described in rat touch domes located at dermatome borders.
source: SAI afferents with overlapping receptive fields have been described in rat touch domes located at dermatome borders (Yasargil et al., 1988; Casserly et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yasargil et al., 1988; Casserly et al., 1994.

claim: Human touch domes are proposed to be innervated by distinct types of sensory afferents.
source: Moreover, human touch domes are proposed to be innervated by distinct types of sensory afferents (Reinisch and Tschachler, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinisch and Tschachler, 2005.

claim: In two touch domes, both a typical SAI afferent and a thinly myelinated, unbranched afferent that contacted Merkel cells were observed.
source: In two touch domes, we observed both a typical SAI afferent and a thinly myelinated, unbranched afferent that contacted Merkel cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from reconstructions.

claim: The thinly myelinated, unbranched afferents observed are speculated to be Aδ afferents based on their thin myelin sheaths and axonal diameters.
source: We speculate that these are Aδ afferents based on their thin myelin sheaths and axonal diameters.
evidence: This is a speculation based on morphological observations.

claim: In monkey and human fingerpads, SAI afferents have non-uniform receptive fields with multiple hot spots that display higher firing rates than surrounding areas.
source: In monkey and human fingerpads, SAI afferents have non-uniform receptive fields with multiple hot spots that display higher firing rates than surrounding areas (Phillips et al., 1992; Vallbo et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 1992; Vallbo et al., 1995.

claim: Hot spots can explain why the resolution of primate SAI afferents is smaller than their receptive field sizes.
source: These hot spots can explain why the resolution of primate SAI afferents is smaller than their receptive field sizes (Phillips et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Phillips et al., 1992.

claim: Johnson and colleagues hypothesized that hot spots correlate with the locations of individual Merkel cell–neurite complexes.
source: Johnson and colleagues hypothesized that hot spots correlate with the locations of individual Merkel cell–neurite complexes; however, their observations of 3–5 hot spots per receptive field in primates (Phillips et al., 1992) coincides well with our finding of 2–6 heminodes per touch-dome SAI afferent.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work, supported by citation to Phillips et al., 1992.

claim: The structural basis of a receptive-field hot spot is proposed to be a cluster of Merkel cell–neurite complexes at a heminode.
source: Thus, we propose that the structural basis of a receptive-field hot spot is a cluster of Merkel cell–neurite complexes at a heminode.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the study's findings and comparison with previous work.

claim: Individual SAI afferents are capable of representing shapes, edges and curvature with high fidelity.
source: Individual SAI afferents are capable of representing shapes, edges and curvature with high fidelity (Johnson and Lamb, 1981; Phillips and Johnson, 1981; Johnson and Hsiao, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and Lamb, 1981; Phillips and Johnson, 1981; Johnson and Hsiao, 1992.

claim: Touch-evoked firing rates, first spike latencies and mechanical sensitivity varied widely between SAI afferents in mouse touch domes.
source: Instead, touch-evoked firing rates, first spike latencies and mechanical sensitivity varied widely between SAI afferents in mouse touch domes, which corroborates previous reports of SAI afferent-to-afferent variability in monkey and human fingerpads (Phillips and Johnson, 1981; Goodwin et al., 1995, 1997; Goodwin and Wheat, 1999).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the study, corroborated by citations.

claim: Variability in firing properties is likely to be a general feature of mammalian SAI afferents.
source: Thus, this variability is likely to be a general feature of mammalian SAI afferents.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of findings across species.

claim: Simulated population responses predict that differences in firing properties will distort the representation of an object's spatial features.
source: Simulated population responses predict that such differences will distort the representation of an object's spatial features (Goodwin and Wheat, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodwin and Wheat, 1999.

claim: The central nervous system might introduce a scaling factor to compensate for peripheral distortion.
source: It is possible that the central nervous system introduces a scaling factor to compensate for peripheral distortion (Goodwin et al., 1995; Goodwin and Wheat, 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to Goodwin et al., 1995; Goodwin and Wheat, 1999.

claim: Having a variety of SAI-afferent sensitivities might extend the dynamic range of the SAI-population response to sustained pressure.
source: For example, having a variety of SAI-afferent sensitivities might extend the dynamic range of the SAI-population response to sustained pressure.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variability.

claim: Variability in SAI end-organ structure is proposed to be the outcome of homeostatic mechanisms engaged during normal skin remodeling.
source: We propose that variability in SAI end-organ structure observed in this study is the outcome of homeostatic mechanisms engaged during normal skin remodeling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the study's findings.

claim: Merkel cells renew within touch domes and whisker follicles.
source: Merkel cells renew within touch domes and whisker follicles (Van Keymeulen et al., 2009; Woo et al., 2010; Doucet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Van Keymeulen et al., 2009; Woo et al., 2010; Doucet et al., 2013.

claim: Hair-growth cycles are accompanied by innervation changes.
source: Moreover, hair-growth cycles are accompanied by innervation changes (Peters et al., 2001; Shimomura and Christiano, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Peters et al., 2001; Shimomura and Christiano, 2010.

claim: SAI-afferent arbors with their Merkel-cell complements are speculated to be dynamic throughout adulthood.
source: We speculate that SAI-afferent arbors with their Merkel-cell complements are likewise dynamic throughout adulthood.
evidence: This is a speculation based on observations of Merkel cell renewal and innervation changes.

claim: Altering the number or arrangement of Merkel cells changes touch-evoked firing according to simulations.
source: Our simulations predict that altering the number or arrangement of Merkel cells changes touch-evoked firing.
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling experiments.

claim: The nervous system might employ homeostatic mechanisms to achieve reliable signaling from individual touch receptors.
source: Thus, our findings raise the possibility that the nervous system employs homeostatic mechanisms to achieve reliable signaling from individual touch receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.
